notes:
Here are the notes, verse by verse. A few verses have thin coverage because I ran out of searches. Verses 3–5 and 23–25 have only one source each, and I found nothing for v. 24. I didn't fetch NetBible notes. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of Philemon, so those are left out.

**Background (several verses)**
- Traditional view: Onesimus ran away from Colossae to Rome, where Paul, in prison, led him to faith. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/how-paul-worked-to-overcome-slavery
- Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey, Demetrius K. Williams) gives three readings: Onesimus was a runaway slave who stole some of Philemon's goods (vv. 15, 18) and ended up in prison with Paul; or he went to Paul on purpose after angering Philemon, so Paul would speak for him; or Philemon or the church sent him to serve Paul in prison. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/onesimus/

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Paul saw himself as Christ's prisoner, not Rome's. In most of his letters he opens by calling himself an "apostle," but here he writes more as a friend. He most likely wrote from Rome (Acts 28), and the Ephesus theory is unlikely. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/
- Catholic view: Philemon was rich and owned slaves. Paul probably converted him at Ephesus. Later tradition makes Philemon Bishop of Colossae and says he was martyred there. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/philemon
- Chrysostom (Orthodox/Catholic church father) says Paul names Timothy too so that Philemon, being entreated by many, may the more readily yield. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23091.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: Apphia was probably Philemon's wife and Archippus probably his son. In that culture the wife ran the household slaves, so the matter concerned her too. The church met in their house. Spurgeon draws from this that every Christian home should be like a church. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/
- Catholic view: Archippus (Col 4:17) held a church office. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/philemon
- Chrysostom: by greeting the whole household church, Paul includes the slaves without naming them, so they won't be jealous and Philemon won't be offended. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23091.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: this is Paul's usual greeting, but here it goes to one person, which makes this a truly personal letter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/

**vv. 4–5**
- Guzik: Paul prayed for Philemon often and with thanks. His faith and love were aimed first at Jesus, then at the saints. "Saints" means every true Christian. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/

**v. 6 (traditions differ on what "sharing/fellowship" means)**
- Reformed (Calvin): faith has a hidden residence in the heart, yet it communicates itself to men by good works. Paul prays that Philemon's faith will prove real by what it does. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philemon/1-6.html
- Wesleyan (Adam Clarke): the word means acts of love and giving to poor Christians. He cites Theophylact, who calls almsgiving the "communication of faith." Same URL.
- Pentecostal/Calvary Chapel (Guzik): mainly about evangelism. Sharing the faith works best when we know and can tell the good God has done in us. He also allows the giving reading. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/
- Ellicott (Anglican): better translated "fellowship in faith." It is fellowship with both God and other people, growing into full knowledge. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/philemon-1.html
- Bob Utley (Baptist) lists three readings: fellowship among believers, sharing the gospel with unbelievers, or sharing good things with others. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philemon/1-6.html
- Chrysostom: faith works when it is accompanied with works. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23092.htm

**v. 7**
- Chrysostom: by praising Philemon's kindness to others, Paul gently prepares him to show the same kindness to Paul. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23092.htm
- Guzik: Philemon met other believers' needs and refreshed them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/

**vv. 8–9 (dispute over "aged")**
- Guzik: Paul could give orders but chooses a loving appeal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/
- Old man or ambassador? The two Greek words differ by one letter. Lightfoot, and Vine's dictionary, read "ambassador." https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/ved/a/aged.html
- Barclay keeps "old man" because Paul is appealing only to love, not to his office. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philemon/1-10.html
- Utley notes all Greek manuscripts have "the aged". https://bible.org/book/export/html/21406
- Calvin (Reformed) takes "elder" to mean not age, but office. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philemon/1-9.html
- 1517 (Lutheran): "elderly man" describes his age but also points to his role as an ambassador. https://www.1517.org/articles/the-gospel-according-to-pauls-letter-to-philemon

**v. 10**
- Guzik: Paul often calls his converts his children. An ancient Greek law, kept by the Romans, let a runaway slave take refuge at an altar or family hearth while the head of the house tried to make peace with the master. Paul is doing something similar. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/
- Chrysostom (Orthodox/Catholic): Onesimus there also received Baptism, which Chrysostom reads from "whom I have begotten in my bonds." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23090.htm

**v. 11**
- Wordplay: the name Onesimus means "useful." https://www.gotquestions.org/Onesimus-in-the-Bible.html
- Guzik: Paul hints he would like to keep Onesimus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/
- Chrysostom: by admitting the slave's faults up front, Paul calms the master's anger. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23092.htm

**v. 12**
- Guzik: running away was wrong and had to be put right. Roman masters had total power, and runaways could be crucified or branded. That is why Paul calls Onesimus "my own heart." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/
- Catholic view: as a Christian, Onesimus was bound to make restitution. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/philemon

**vv. 13–14**
- Guzik: Paul's request is strong, but he truly leaves the choice to Philemon, so the good deed will be freely given. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/
- Chrysostom draws a lesson that we ought not to withdraw slaves from the service of their masters. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23090.htm

**v. 15**
- Guzik: "separated for a while" is a gentle way to describe running away. "Perhaps" shows Paul is not claiming to know God's hidden plan for sure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/

**v. 16 (slavery and emancipation)**
- Guzik and F. F. Bruce: the letter puts slavery where it could only wilt and die, because how can a brother be a slave? https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/
- Piper (Baptist): the brother relationship replaces the slave relationship. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/how-paul-worked-to-overcome-slavery
- Steven Cole (bible.org): we don't know whether Philemon freed him, but they now related on a new basis. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21861
- Catholic view: Paul doesn't directly ask for freedom. It quotes Lightfoot: "emancipation seems to be trembling on his lips." https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/philemon
- Chrysostom: Philemon gains a brother for ever. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23092.htm
- Bible Odyssey: the meaning depends on Paul's ambiguous wording. Does Onesimus stay a slave, go back to serve Paul, or get legally freed? https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/onesimus/

**v. 17**
- Wiersbe: "receive him as me" reminds us we are "accepted in the Beloved". https://www.preceptaustin.org/philemon-devotionals
- Chrysostom: "if you consider me a friend." https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23093.htm

**v. 18 (imputation)**
- Barnes: the verb used is the same word as "imputed" in Romans 5:13. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philemon/1-18.html
- Lutheran: quotes Luther that Paul does for Onesimus what Christ does for us with the Father. https://www.1517.org/articles/the-gospel-according-to-pauls-letter-to-philemon
- Precept Austin calls it the best New Testament picture of substitutionary atonement. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philemon-commentary
- Clarke (Wesleyan) stresses the "if": Paul is only describing a possibility. Haydock (Catholic) says "as he confesses". https://www.studylight.org/commentary/philemon/1-18.html
- Chrysostom: Paul says "wronged," not "stolen," to avoid stirring up anger. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23093.htm

**v. 19**
- Paul gives Philemon a written promise to pay. "You owe me yourself" means Philemon was saved through Paul's ministry. https://bible.org/article/what-biblical-imputation-think-about-it-and-take-it-credit
- Chrysostom: you owe me Not only your own things, but yourself also. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23093.htm

**vv. 20–21**
- Chrysostom: "Yea, brother" carries an unspoken "receive him." Paul writes with confidence, not as a command. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23093.htm

**v. 22**
- Precept Austin: Paul's plan to pay suggests he expected to be released, as this request for lodging also shows. https://www.preceptaustin.org/philemon-commentary
- Chrysostom: Philemon's house was altogether a lodging for the Saints. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23090.htm

**v. 23**
- Chrysostom: Epaphras was sent by the Colossians, which shows Philemon lived at Colossae. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23093.htm

**v. 25**
- Guzik: the bishop of Ephesus around A.D. 110 was named Onesimus and could have been the same man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/philemon-1/
- Catholic tradition instead makes Onesimus Bishop of Beroea. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/philemon
